title: Command of Evidence: Textual
lead: These questions state a claim about a subject you have probably never met and ask which choice gives the strongest evidence for it. Each one is a single question with its own short text. You need no background knowledge: everything required is in the passage.

parts.title: Part 1 · Two kinds of evidence question
parts.html:
Scientific evidenceLiterary evidence
The passage givesA hypothesis from science or social science, usually with a description of a studyA claim about a poem, novel or other literary work
The choices arePossible findings or resultsQuotations from the work
Your taskPick the result you would expect to see if the hypothesis were truePick the quotation that directly shows what the claim says
Typical question“Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?”“Which quotation most effectively illustrates the claim?”

The first is what you do in a science class when you check an experiment against a hypothesis. The second is what you do in a literature essay when you choose a quotation to back up a point. They look different, but the same three steps solve both.

In both, the claim is handed to you. Your job is not to interpret the passage; it is to find the choice that demonstrates that exact claim. Every choice will be on topic. Only one proves the claim.

parts.title: Part 2 · The three-step method
parts.html:
1. Identify the argument. Find the claim the evidence has to support and separate it from the rest of the text. It may be a hypothesis or an interpretation of a literary work, and it is always stated outright.
  2. Make a test phrase. Reduce the claim to the simplest wording you can, a few words that keep its key parts. “Good writers write for general readers” must keep both the writers and that audience; evidence about only one of them does not prove it.
  3. Test the choices. Hold each choice against the test phrase. If it says something different, eliminate it. The choice that says the same thing as your test phrase is the answer.

parts.title: Part 3 · Worked example: a scientific hypothesis
parts.html:
Jan Gimsa, Robert Sleigh, and Ulrike Gimsa have hypothesized that the sail-like structure running down the back of the dinosaur Spinosaurus aegyptiacus improved the animal’s success in underwater pursuits of prey species capable of making quick, evasive movements. To evaluate their hypothesis, a second team of researchers constructed two battery-powered mechanical models of S. aegyptiacus, one with a sail and one without, and subjected the models to a series of identical tests in a water-filled tank. Which finding from the model tests, if true, would most strongly support Gimsa and colleagues’ hypothesis?
A) The model with a sail took significantly longer to travel a specified distance while submerged than the model without a sail did.
B) The model with a sail displaced significantly more water while submerged than the model without a sail did.
C) The model with a sail had significantly less battery power remaining after completing the tests than the model without a sail did.
D) The model with a sail took significantly less time to complete a sharp turn while submerged than the model without a sail did.

Identify the argument. The hypothesis is the first sentence: the sail helped the dinosaur catch prey that makes quick, evasive movements underwater.

Make a test phrase. “Sail = quicker, more agile movement underwater.”

Test the choices.

  • A is about speed, but it says the sail made the model slower. That is the opposite direction.
  • B is about how much water was displaced, not about how quickly the model moved.
  • C is about battery power used, not about how quickly the model moved.
  • D says the model with a sail made a sharp turn in less time. Sharp, fast turns are exactly what chasing evasive prey needs, so it matches the test phrase. D is the answer.

parts.title: Part 4 · Three ways a choice fails
parts.html:
For each choice, ask: “what claim would this prove?” If the answer is not the claim in the question, the choice is out, however relevant it sounds.

  • Wrong support: it proves a different claim.
  • Too weak: it points toward the idea without showing it. “She enjoyed experimenting” does not prove her early work was innovative; being open to new ideas is a different claim.
  • Wrong scope: it proves more or less than was asked. If the claim is about one character’s unused talent, a quotation about a gloomy landscape sets a mood but does not show it.

Literary questions have their own traps.

  • Mood is not evidence. Do not pick a quotation because it feels like the claim. Pick the one where a character’s words or actions show it.
  • Check who is being described. In a poem such as “To Autumn”, lines that sound as if they describe a person may be addressed to the season. The sentence that introduces the text tells you who or what is meant.

parts.title: Part 5 · Worked example: a quotation
parts.html:
Critics initially dismissed the poet's work. Decades later, scholars reevaluated it and concluded that her unconventional line breaks were deliberate innovations. One scholar argued the line breaks were not merely stylistic quirks; they were her method for controlling pacing and emphasis.

Claim to support. The poet's line breaks were purposeful rather than accidental.
QuoteVerdict
A) “Critics initially dismissed the poet's work.”On-topic, but proves dismissal, not purpose.
B) “…they were her method for controlling pacing and emphasis.”Correct. States the purpose and includes the mechanism.
C) “…her unconventional line breaks were deliberate innovations.”Supportive but weaker. “Deliberate” shows intent without showing what the breaks accomplished.

B and C both point the right way, and precision picks B. When two choices both look supportive, choose the one that states the claim directly and completely, including the mechanism or reason and not only the conclusion.

parts.title: Part 6 · Tips that save points
parts.html:
TipHow to use it
Be strictIf a choice only “sort of” feels like evidence, eliminate it. If you have to connect several dots yourself to make it fit the claim, it is not strong evidence.
Stay specificDo not go beyond what the passage covers. Reject choices that widen or blur its ideas, and watch for a small twist that makes a choice sound relevant while saying something the passage does not support.
Read the question for directionMost questions ask what would support the claim. Some ask what would undermine, weaken or challenge it, and then you need the finding that disagrees with the claim. One wrong choice is usually the right answer for the opposite direction.

A finding supports a hypothesis when it is what you would expect to see if the hypothesis were true. It weakens the hypothesis when it is the opposite of what you would expect.

parts.title: Part 7 · Predict the evidence; weaken questions
parts.html:
Write the claim as an arrow. Most hypotheses say that one thing produces or goes with another. Reduce the claim to that: “more X → more Y”.

Then predict the evidence before reading the choices. The choices are written to confuse, and a prediction keeps you steady.

Question asks forLook for a finding where
SupportX and Y appear together as the claim says: the group with more X has more Y
Weaken (undermine)X is present and Y is not; or Y appears without X; or the opposite of the predicted result occurs

A weaken question uses exactly the same steps as a support question. Only the direction of the last step changes.

Example. Great tits living in cities sing at a higher pitch than those in forests. Some biologists hypothesize that the birds raise their pitch because low-pitched traffic noise drowns out low notes.

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the biologists' hypothesis? A) Great tits beside busy roads sing at a higher pitch than great tits in quiet city parks.
B) City great tits sing at the same pitch on streets closed to traffic as on busy streets.
C) Several other bird species also live in both cities and forests.
D) Traffic noise in most cities is loudest in the early morning. Arrow: traffic noise ↑ → pitch ↑.
Prediction for “weaken”: noise changes and pitch does not.
A shows noise and pitch rising together, so it supports the hypothesis. C and D are about the topic and say nothing about pitch.
B matches the prediction: the noise is gone and the pitch is the same.
  • Check the direction last. Before you confirm, reread the question for “support” or “weaken”. In a weaken question, the best supporting finding is always among the choices, as A is here.
  • Do not untangle a choice that will not connect. If you cannot see after one careful reading how a choice bears on the arrow, it probably does not bear on it. Spending a minute building a link is a sign that the choice is wrong.
  • Both halves of the arrow must be in the evidence. A choice about traffic noise alone, or pitch alone, cannot support or weaken a claim about how the two are linked.
